spot.v: A milky or viscous film. On shiitake, a moist film on the outside of the block, like frost on the inside of the bag.
A sour smell (dirty socks, fermenting wine), sometimes noticed through the patch. Blocks colonize weakly, wispy or greasy, and many species do not fruit.

look.v: Strong top and weak bottom is the stratified pattern (short hold). Hard line over a sloppy wet bottom is pooled water.

cause.v: Steam kills active bacteria, but they make heat-resistant endospores; fungi do not. Ultra-pasteurization (about 100 °C / 212 °F) is not sterilization, so spores stay in every block and wake only if conditions allow.

Heat: thermophile spores take hold around 24 °C (75 °F), and a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block core runs 2-3 °C (4-5 °F) above the room. Cores above about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F) go wrong. Heat plus high CO2 feed each other.
Too wet (above about 62-68% moisture), a cook too short, slow cooling in or around the vessel, blocks left days before inoculation, a mix that was fermenting, or a media too rich.

treat.v: Throw sour-smelling blocks away. If it came from the substrate, check cook time and temperature, whether the mix ferments, and how long it sat before processing and before inoculation.

prevent.v: Incubate at about 19 °C (66 °F) room air so big-block cores stay under about 21-22 °C. Moisture at or below the species target. Cool hot and inoculate promptly at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F).
Check the data-logger record first when blocks go bad.

risk.v: Shiitake: heat-driven anaerobic bacteria are a main incubation failure; the block can look fine and fail late.
Lion's mane: over-spawning and heat bring bacteria. Maitake on rich 50:50 media gets heavy metabolites.

spot.v: A hard line of mycelium above a sloppy, wet bottom. Water pools at the bottom and goes airless. Sour smell.
Strong colonization at the top and weak at the bottom of the block.

look.v: A short cook gives the same strong-top, weak-bottom picture on big blocks. Check the core temperature log to tell them apart.

cause.v: Too much water pooled. Above about 62% moisture, lion's mane blocks pool water at the bottom.
Overly wet shiitake (strain KOM) goes anaerobic with popcorning and browning only on top, but still fruits; 3790 gives sloshy blocks that fruit poorly.

treat.v: Reduce water and even out hydration. Aim for no moisture difference between top and bottom.

prevent.v: Test the moisture of incoming sawdust before changing the recipe.

risk.v: Lion's mane and shiitake are the named cases.

spot.v: Yellow liquid at the bottom of a bag, more with rich 50:50 lion's mane blocks. Also seen during fruiting.

look.v: Yellow or orange metabolites on older shiitake, chestnut and pioppino grain are normal. Heavy exudate in a block is not.

cause.v: Working explanation: a core or room too hot lets dormant endospores wake, conditions go wet and airless, and the mycelium pumps out defensive metabolites.
Heavy metabolite formation (except shiitake, which makes them normally) means media too rich or undercooked. Bacteria may then stop fruiting entirely.

treat.v: Cooler incubation and a leaner mix (soy about 30-40%).

prevent.v: Lean mix, correct cook, steady cool room.

risk.v: Lion's mane; rich maitake blocks wick exudate up into the fruit.

name: DARK WET SPOTS AT INOCULATION POINTS

spot.v: Dark, wet circular spots around each inoculation point.

look.v: Poor shaking gives patchy colonization and hot grain clumps. Check how the spawn was spread before blaming bacteria.

cause.v: Over-spawning makes extra heat and more bacteria. Overheating can kill the mycelium in ultra-pasteurized substrate.

treat.v: Lower the spawn rate. Shake thoroughly.

prevent.v: Keep spawn at the set rate (about 20 blocks per 6 lb G2 bag).

risk.v: Lion's mane is the named case.

spot.v: The spawn dies. The bottom to middle goes gnarly with bacteria, perhaps with mould on top. The crop forms dense walled-off struggling colonies, not fast feathery rope-like growth.
Weak, wispy, greasy colonization, and many species (even reishi) never fruit.

look.v: If the spawn never grows, or only a few nodules, it was killed at 38 °C (100 °F) or more. That is not contamination.

cause.v: Hot blocks sat 1-3 days before reaching a filtered cool-down room, or were knocked too hot, or the block fermented before inoculation.
Pasteurized blocks have an expiry. Left days, endospores germinate and the block ferments with a sour smell.

treat.v: Discard the blocks. Move hot blocks straight into a filtered cool-down room and inoculate promptly at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F).

prevent.v: Inoculate promptly once blocks reach 27-32 °C. Never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.

risk.v: All species. Case: a Midwest farm where many species, even reishi, would not fruit.

name: FERMENTED GRAIN
aka: SPLOTCHY GRAIN AFTER A LONG SOAK

spot.v: Irregular, splotchy colonization on grain even after sterilization.

look.v: Burst grain feeds bacteria like agar. Mushy kernels and standing water are the sign, not splotches alone.

cause.v: A long soak, or drained grain left standing, starts fermenting (sugars to alcohols). Long soaks are not needed to kill endospores.
Grain that is too wet gives mushy burst grain and standing water that breed contaminants.

treat.v: Discard. Shorten the soak and process promptly.

prevent.v: Hydrate fully and evenly but stop short of bursting. Drain and cook without waiting.

spot.v: Heavy exudate, sectoring (uneven wedges instead of one front) and wet spots in the block.

look.v: Shiitake makes metabolites normally. Yellow or orange droplets on older grain are normal.

cause.v: Poorly mixed or wrongly hydrated substrate, temperature swings in incubation, or competitors, even with good steaming.

treat.v: Homogeneous mix and a stable room. Leaner mix or a better cook.

prevent.v: Mix well, hydrate by measure, hold room temperature steady.

risk.v: Species other than shiitake. Rich maitake blocks wick exudate into the fruit.

name: BLACK SLIME ON LION'S MANE STEMS

spot.v: Black slime on lion's mane stems.

look.v: Probably a different bacterium from classic blotch.

cause.v: Not pinned down in the sources. Lion's mane does worse when too hot, with more bacterial infection.

prevent.v: Keep lion's mane near 16 °C (60 °F) (HeCNS sweet spot); treat humidifier water.

spot.v: Young fruits turn white with a cauliflower-like look instead of darkening.

look.v: Normal maitake darkens as it grows. White cauliflower is the warning.

cause.v: Bacteria not killed without pressure in ultra-pasteurized blocks, worse when bags are put to fruit too early.

treat.v: Wait longer before fruiting. Consider sterilizing.

prevent.v: Do not rush maitake to fruit. Leaner mix than 50:50 where exudate wicks into fruit.
